title: Agitation at the Community Clinic
objective: Students recognise lithium toxicity beneath a manic presentation, link it to dehydration, withhold the drug, escalate, and evaluate the response.
endpoint: Stabilisation after overnight hospital treatment, clinic review, and client and family education

opening.narrative: Tanisha, a 34-year-old woman, is brought to the community mental health clinic by her sister after five days of sleeping very little, talking rapidly, and spending a large sum of money at the market. Her sister states, "She has not been herself. She argues with everyone and will not sit down." History includes bipolar disorder, treated with lithium carbonate taken at 10 am and 10 pm. Two weeks ago her dose was increased from 300 mg to 450 mg twice daily because she had begun sleeping less. She has no other prescribed medication and no known drug allergies. She lives with her sister and works at a grocery. The clinic's standing orders allow the registered nurse to withhold a prescribed dose and notify the physician when a drug level is markedly abnormal.

stages.narrative: The nurse completes the initial assessment and sends blood for a serum lithium level at 9:40 am.

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented. Coarse tremor of both hands. Walks with an unsteady, wide-based gait.
Speech rapid and difficult to interrupt. Moves constantly in the chair.

stages.narrative: The sister adds that Tanisha has had two days of vomiting, has kept little down, and has been drinking very little fluid. She took her 10 pm lithium dose last night.
The serum lithium result is reported. The sample was taken about 12 hours after last night's dose. Tanisha's 10:00 am lithium dose is now due, and the physician is being contacted by telephone.

The physician confirms that lithium is to be withheld and arranges overnight admission to the district hospital for intravenous fluids, with urine output and electrolytes monitored. A clinic review is booked for the next morning, after discharge from hospital.
Tanisha is discharged from the district hospital early in the morning and attends the clinic review with her sister. She received intravenous fluids overnight, and lithium was withheld.

assessment.finding: Hand tremor much reduced since yesterday. Gait steady.
Urine output since yesterday approximately 50 mL/hr.
Slept six hours overnight. Still speaks rapidly but sits calmly during the interview.

stages.narrative: The sister quietly tells the nurse, "I love her, but I honestly cannot manage another week like the last one at home."
The physician restarts lithium at a lower dose, with a repeat level booked in five days. As she prepares to go home, Tanisha asks the nurse, "What can I do to stop this from happening again?"

questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse recognize as requiring immediate follow-up?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulse of 104/min while seated

options.label: B
options.text: Coarse hand tremor with unsteady gait

options.label: C
options.text: Blood pressure of 138/88 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.text: Irritability with reduced sleep

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Tanisha takes lithium, a drug with a narrow therapeutic range, and her dose was raised two weeks ago. A fine tremor is common at usual levels, but a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait is a neurological sign of a rising lithium level, so it needs follow-up now. The rest of the picture (restlessness, rapid speech, reduced sleep) is explained by the mania her sister describes.

distractor_rationales.A: A pulse of 104/min fits her agitation and constant movement. It should be rechecked, but it does not point to a medication-safety problem the way the tremor and gait do.
distractor_rationales.C: A blood pressure of 138/88 mm Hg is only slightly raised and fits her agitation. Rechecking it later is reasonable; it is not the finding that needs action first.
distractor_rationales.D: Irritability and reduced sleep are the presenting manic picture already reported by her sister at 9:15 am, so they add nothing new requiring immediate follow-up.

questions.self_test: The pulse of 104/min is explained by agitation, whereas a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait in a client taking lithium signals a rising drug level.

meta.priority_principle: Medication safety cue over expected disease features
meta.prerequisites: Lithium therapeutic index; fine versus coarse tremor; signs of mania
meta.suggested_review: Lithium adverse effects and toxicity signs

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret the significance of the vomiting and low fluid intake for Tanisha's tremor?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid and sodium loss reduce lithium excretion, so the level rises

options.label: B
options.text: Vomiting has reduced lithium absorption, so the level is likely low

options.label: C
options.text: Dehydration alone is causing the tremor and needs replacing first

options.label: D
options.text: The tremor reflects anxiety about the vomiting, not the medication

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The kidneys reabsorb lithium by the same route as sodium. Two days of vomiting and little fluid have left Tanisha short of fluid and sodium, so her kidneys hold on to sodium and lithium with it. Together with the dose increase two weeks ago, this explains how her level could rise and produce the coarse tremor and unsteady gait.

distractor_rationales.B: Vomiting soon after a dose can lose some of it, which is why this is tempting. But two days of poor intake on a recently increased dose make accumulation the danger, and a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait points to a high level, not a low one.
distractor_rationales.C: Dehydration does need correcting, but it is the reason lithium is accumulating, not the cause of the tremor itself. Treating it as the whole explanation misses the drug level.
distractor_rationales.D: Anxiety can cause a fine tremor, but not a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait, and the vomiting and low intake give a clear drug-related explanation.

questions.self_test: Less lithium absorbed sounds logical, but the kidneys retaining more lithium during fluid and sodium loss is what makes the level rise.

meta.priority_principle: Link new cues to the drug's known risks
meta.prerequisites: Sodium and lithium reabsorption in the kidney

questions.stem: Before the lithium result is available, which condition is most likely and should be prioritized?

options.label: A
options.text: Relapse of a manic episode

options.label: B
options.text: Lithium toxicity

options.label: C
options.text: Gastroenteritis with dehydration

options.label: D
options.text: Overactive thyroid gland

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: A recently increased lithium dose, two days of vomiting with poor intake, and a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait form one picture: lithium toxicity. It is also the most dangerous possibility, because it can progress to confusion, seizures and kidney injury, so it is prioritized while the level is awaited.

distractor_rationales.A: Her behaviour does support a manic relapse, which is why this is the classic trap. Relapse does not explain the coarse tremor and unsteady gait, and it is not immediately dangerous; toxicity is.
distractor_rationales.C: Gastroenteritis explains the vomiting and is why the level may have risen, so it is a contributing cause to treat. It does not explain the neurological signs by itself.
distractor_rationales.D: An overactive thyroid can cause tremor, a fast pulse and agitation, but not an unsteady gait with vomiting, and it does not account for the recent lithium dose increase.

questions.self_test: Manic relapse explains the behaviour but not a coarse tremor and unsteady gait after vomiting on a recently increased lithium dose.

meta.priority_principle: Life-threatening problem before the expected illness

questions.stem: Which intervention should the nurse anticipate in Tanisha's plan of care?

options.label: A
options.text: IV fluids with monitoring of urine output and electrolytes

options.label: B
options.text: Oral fluids at home with a repeat lithium level next week

options.label: C
options.text: A low-sodium diet to bring the blood pressure down

options.label: D
options.text: Activated charcoal to bind the lithium in her stomach

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: A level of 2.0 mmol/L taken 12 hours after a dose is well above the usual maintenance range (roughly 0.6 to 1.2 mmol/L) and matches her neurological signs. She is fluid- and sodium-depleted, which is why her kidneys are holding on to lithium. Restoring fluid and sodium intravenously increases lithium excretion, and urine output and electrolytes show whether the plan is working.

distractor_rationales.B: Rehydration is the right idea, but she has been vomiting for two days and has signs of toxicity, so oral fluids at home with a check next week are too little and too late.
distractor_rationales.C: Reducing sodium makes the kidneys reabsorb more lithium and would raise the level further. Her blood pressure is not the problem being treated.
distractor_rationales.D: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium, and her last dose was 12 hours ago, so it would not lower the level. Removing lithium depends on the kidneys.

questions.self_test: Oral fluids at home address the dehydration but are too slow and too unmonitored for a level of 2.0 mmol/L with neurological signs.

meta.priority_principle: Correct the cause and monitor the response
meta.suggested_review: Fluid and electrolyte management in lithium toxicity

questions.stem: The physician has not yet been reached and the 10:00 am dose is due. Which action should the nurse perform first?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the 10:00 am dose while awaiting the physician's reply

options.label: B
options.text: Encourage oral fluids at home and reassess in the morning

options.label: C
options.text: Hold the 10:00 am dose and report the level and findings

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the lithium level before deciding about the dose

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The clinic's standing orders allow the nurse to withhold a dose when a level is markedly abnormal. Holding the 10:00 am dose stops more lithium entering a toxic client, and reporting the level, tremor, gait and vomiting gives the physician what is needed to order treatment.

distractor_rationales.A: Giving lithium at a level of 2.0 mmol/L with neurological signs adds to the toxicity and risks seizures. Waiting for the physician is not a reason to give it.
distractor_rationales.B: Sending her home with oral fluids delays treatment of a toxic level and leaves the physician uninformed.
distractor_rationales.D: The level was taken correctly, 12 hours after a dose, and matches her signs. Repeating it delays the decision while the dose is due now; holding the dose and reporting comes first.

questions.self_test: Repeating the level feels careful, but the result already fits her signs and the dose is due now, so holding it and reporting comes first.

meta.subtopic: Holding a dose under standing orders
meta.suggested_review: When a nurse may withhold a prescribed dose

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that management of the primary problem is effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Falling lithium level with less tremor

options.label: B
options.text: Sister reports that Tanisha's mood seems brighter

options.label: C
options.text: Sleeping six hours overnight

options.label: D
options.text: Blood pressure of 128/80 mm Hg

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The problem being treated was lithium toxicity, so the outcome measures are the lithium level and the toxicity sign. The level has fallen from 2.0 to 1.1 mmol/L and the tremor is much reduced after fluids and withholding the drug.

distractor_rationales.B: A brighter mood is welcome, but mood changes slowly and reflects the bipolar illness, not whether the toxicity has been treated.
distractor_rationales.C: Better sleep is a positive sign of settling mania, but it does not measure the toxicity that the fluids and withheld dose were treating.
distractor_rationales.D: Her blood pressure was never the problem being managed, so its improvement does not show that the toxicity treatment worked.

questions.self_test: Brighter mood is true but measures the manic illness, not the toxicity that the fluids and withheld doses were treating.

meta.priority_principle: Evaluate the outcome the intervention targeted

questions.stem: Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: "That sounds exhausting. Tell me what a typical day has been like at home."

options.label: B
options.text: "She will settle once the medication takes effect, so give it a little more time."

options.label: C
options.text: "Would it help if we arranged for her to be admitted so you can rest?"

options.label: D
options.text: "Try to stay positive, because your attitude will influence her recovery."

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The sister is telling the nurse she is close to her limit. Acknowledging that feeling and asking what a typical day looks like keeps her talking and shows the nurse what support is needed (sleep, safety, money), which matters in the Caribbean where family is usually the main carer.

distractor_rationales.B: This offers reassurance with an uncertain timeline and passes over the strain she has just described.
distractor_rationales.C: Admission or respite may be needed, but offering a solution before understanding her situation is premature.
distractor_rationales.D: This puts the responsibility for Tanisha's recovery on her sister's attitude, which can add guilt to her exhaustion.

questions.self_test: Offering admission may be needed later, but it jumps to a solution before the nurse understands what the sister is struggling with.

meta.suggested_review: Carer strain in serious mental illness

questions.stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to provide?

options.label: A
options.text: Use ibuprofen rather than paracetamol for aches and pains

options.label: B
options.text: Keep your fluid and salt intake consistent every day

options.label: C
options.text: If you miss a dose, take two tablets at the next dose time

options.label: D
options.text: Choose low-sodium foods to protect your heart long-term

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: This episode happened because vomiting and poor intake lowered her fluid and sodium, so her kidneys kept more lithium. Keeping fluid and salt intake steady every day is the measure she controls that most directly prevents it happening again.

distractor_rationales.A: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs reduce lithium excretion and can push the level up; paracetamol is the safer choice for minor pain.
distractor_rationales.C: Doubling up after a missed dose produces a peak in the lithium level and risks toxicity; the missed dose should be skipped or taken as advised.
distractor_rationales.D: Low-sodium advice sounds healthy, but cutting sodium increases lithium reabsorption, so it would make another episode more likely.

questions.self_test: Low-sodium eating is good general advice, but for a client on lithium it raises the drug level, so it is the wrong teaching here.

meta.priority_principle: Teach the cause the client controls

pathophysiology:
## Pathophysiology teaching

Lithium is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. In the proximal tubule it is reabsorbed by the same pathways as sodium, so the body cannot tell the two apart.

Tanisha's dose had been increased two weeks earlier, which raised her level towards the top of the range. When she then vomited for two days and drank very little, she lost fluid and sodium. Her kidneys responded by reabsorbing more sodium to protect her circulating volume, and they reabsorbed more lithium with it. Her serum level rose to 2.0 mmol/L.

**Timing the level.** Lithium levels are read about 12 hours after the last dose. A sample taken a few hours after a dose reads falsely high, which is why the case states when the sample was taken.

**Signs.** A fine hand tremor is common at usual levels. As the level rises, it becomes a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait, then confusion, seizures and coma, and lithium can injure the kidney further, which slows clearance again. Mania and toxicity can occur together: the illness that prompted the dose increase has not yet settled, which is why her behaviour hides the drug problem.

**Why each decision mattered.**
- Recognising the coarse tremor and unsteady gait (Q1) and linking the vomiting to lithium retention (Q2) pointed to the drug, not the illness.
- Prioritizing toxicity over a manic relapse before the result (Q3) meant the level was read as confirmation, not a surprise.
- Holding the dose (Q5) stopped more drug entering the body; intravenous fluids (Q4) restored sodium and volume so the kidneys could excrete lithium again.
- Urine output, sodium and potassium on day 2 confirm that the kidneys are clearing lithium and the fluid replacement is adequate.
- The level and tremor improve within a day; mood settles over days to weeks, which is why mood and sleep are not the measures of toxicity treatment (Q6).

**Prevention.** Steady fluid and salt intake, avoiding NSAIDs and diuretics unless prescribed with monitoring, never doubling a missed dose, extra level checks after any dose change, and seeking help early when vomiting or diarrhoea stops a client keeping fluids down.
quality_report: Revised by Claude (2026-10-08) from Jade's Lithium Toxicity draft, at Ian's request, to meet V3 and the error-prevention addendum: Q4 changed from 'withhold the next dose' (duplicating Q5's key) to anticipating IV fluids with urine-output and electrolyte monitoring; a 10:30 am stage added so the IV fluids evaluated in Q6 are introduced first (V3 s.6); implausible distractors replaced (Q4 'increase the dose', Q5 'arrange transport before informing anyone', Q8 'stop lithium once stable'); Q1 rationale explains why the tremor is the safety cue. Cover, two-answer, cue-sufficiency and hidden-assumption checks were re-run on all eight items. Pending Jade's review and clinical validation (lithium thresholds, standing-order scope, Caribbean facility norms). Flow revision (Claude, 2026-10-09, at Ian's request): stages reordered so no question is answered by the screen before it (Q3 now asked before the lithium result; the standing-order wording moved to the opening; Q2 now analyses the vomiting cue). Clinical consistency: dose increased two weeks earlier explains mania with toxicity; coarse tremor and unsteady gait replace the fine tremor to match a level of 2.0 mmol/L; level timed 12 hours post-dose; overnight hospital admission made explicit; Q4 'withhold and repeat in a week' (half-right, overlapped Q5) replaced with activated charcoal; Q5 'half dose' replaced with 'repeat the level'; Q3 'worsening hypertension' replaced with an overactive thyroid.
